issues.legal_issue: A first appellate court cannot rely on additional evidence against a party without giving that party an opportunity to adduce rebuttal evidence.
material_facts: In appeals from the dismissal of four civil suits, the plaintiffs were permitted to introduce additional evidence for the first time at the appellate stage.
The first appellate court relied on that evidence to allow the appeals and decree the suits without giving the defendants an opportunity to present rebuttal evidence.
The defendants were prejudiced by the adverse decision based on evidence they had no opportunity to counter.
issues.conclusion: The first appellate court’s decision on the merits could not be sustained because it relied on additional evidence without giving the opposing party an opportunity to rebut it.
issues.legal_principle: When additional evidence is admitted in an appeal under Order 41 Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the opposing party must have an opportunity to meet that evidence, including by adducing rebuttal evidence. The Court relied on Land Acquisition Officer, City Improvement Trust Board v. H. Narayanaiah, (1976) 4 SCC 9; Shalimar Chemical Works Ltd. v. Surendra Oil & Dal Mills (Refineries), (2010) 8 SCC 423; and Akhilesh Singh v. Lal Babu Singh, (2018) 4 SCC 759.

rule.if: first_appeal and additional_evidence_admitted and not rebuttal_opportunity

predicates.first_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal from a trial court’s decision.
predicates.additional_evidence_admitted: The appellate court admits additional evidence and relies on it in deciding the appeal.
predicates.rebuttal_opportunity: The party opposing the additional evidence is given an opportunity to present evidence to counter it.

issues.definition: When an appellate court in a first appeal relies on additional evidence without giving the opposing party an opportunity to counter it, the appellate merits decision is set aside.

issues.legal_issue: When a first appellate court admits additional evidence and needs further fact-finding to decide the merits, it must use a remand or limited-issue procedure rather than decide the merits without that procedure.
material_facts: The first appellate court admitted additional evidence and relied on it to decide the appeals on their merits.
It neither set aside the trial court’s decision and remanded the suits for retrial nor retained the appeals while referring particular issues for findings by the trial court.
The Supreme Court found that the omission, together with the lack of an opportunity to adduce rebuttal evidence, caused prejudice and constituted jurisdictional error.
issues.conclusion: The first appellate court should have used either a full retrial remand or a limited-issue reference for findings; its failure to do so rendered its merits decision unsustainable. The Supreme Court set aside the appellate merits decision and remanded the suits for retrial.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order 41 Rule 23-A of the Code of Civil Procedure, an appellate court may set aside the trial court’s judgment and remand the case for retrial; under Order 41 Rule 25, it may retain the appeal and refer particular issues to the trial court for findings. Where additional evidence is admitted and further trial-level proceedings are needed, the appellate court must use an appropriate procedure rather than decide the merits without them.

rule.if: first_appeal and additional_evidence_admitted and further_fact_finding_needed and appellate_court_decides_merits_without_trial_procedure

predicates.first_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal from a trial court’s decision.
predicates.additional_evidence_admitted: The appellate court admits additional evidence for consideration in the appeal.
predicates.further_fact_finding_needed: The additional evidence requires trial-level proof or findings before the merits can fairly be decided.
predicates.appellate_court_decides_merits_without_t: The appellate court decides the merits without remanding for retrial or referring issues for trial-court findings.

issues.definition: When a first appellate court admits additional evidence requiring further fact-finding but decides the merits without a remand or issue-reference procedure, its merits decision is set aside and the case is remanded for retrial.
